@zachleat I'd heard the same from my sources. Post-acquisition, I kept telling folks that my expectation was that they'd "donate" it to the OpenJS Foundation or something like that to "give it back to the community" (i.e. we don't maintain it anymore).

That could still happen but the current trajectory looks worse than my prediction.
@remotesynth I appreciate that tough choices are being made but the lack of communication is not a good look

@zachleat I really hate to say this, because I'm acquainted with some of the people involved, but GatsbyJS was/is a tire fire to actually work with.

I wrote a blog post on my experience, and it wasn't pretty. I tried like heck to be as open minded and fair as I could.

https://www.feoh.org/posts/mis-adventures-in-gatsbyjs

#javascript #gatsby #webdev
@feoh yeah the merits of the framework are probably a moot point now

@zachleat Agreed. I know folks on Gatsby Cloud and they keep being told that the features will be rolled into standard Netlify, but I don't see how that aligns with the current plans for putting Gatsby in maintenance mode. I can't see them putting engineering resources on an EOL project.
@remotesynth I don’t think I’m allowed to say but I did play darts last weekend and got a bullseye

@zachleat I dunno. I think they still have a place. I'm building a @djangonews app for myself right now as I need a CRUD thing and I don't want to have to spend months learning something super heavy or alternatively so light I have to build everything from scratch.
@feoh ah, to be clear—specifically I don’t believe the merits of Gatsby are relevant if they are retiring the thing

Perhaps controversially—I believe the same could very easily happen to any VC-funded framework.

What happens when you have multiple FTE on payroll and you exhaust your runway without a viable strategy to monetize?

@zachleat "community stewardship" - always the ideal but almost impossible to find.

I feel for them, and hope they all land on their feet

@brianleroux @boneskull @zachleat This is my favorite takeaway. The reason to target JS was that it was "close to the metal" in terms of portable Web media; the entire cottage industry of "transpiler to JS" is built upon that requirement. I can't help but speculate that WASM is part of the picture; the overwhelming complexity had to collapse somehow, and shifting foundations would be a reasonable cause.

There was discussion about this recently, on Lobsters: https://lobste.rs/s/id9jet/transpiler_meaningless_word

@corbin @boneskull @zachleat text to text is pretty lossy and interpreted code always on a back foot wrt optimization so wasm def seems inevitable.

But I've been saying this for a decade at least now too. I have no issue with the techniques but question their assumed universal application.
